newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Fighting in north Cambodia, foreign exodus goes on.
newsitem.headline: Fighting in north Cambodia, foreign exodus goes on.

text.p: Fighting broke out near the famed Angkor Wat temple complex in northwest Cambodia on Friday as more foreigners streamed out of the strife-torn country.

As the United States announced the temporary suspension of aid in response to the ouster of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, ordinary Cambodians said their dreams of peace and prosperity were slipping away.

A military official loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, speaking by telephone from Siem Reap, 250 km northwest (150 miles) of the capital, said fighting broke out between forces loyal to the rival prime ministers to the west of the town at daybreak on Friday.
He said reinforcements and ammunition were being sent to the area, 30 km (20 miles) west of the town.

Residents in Siem Reap, home to the 12th century Angkor Wat temple complex, said shelling was audible but the town, which is under the control of forces loyal to powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, was quiet but tense.
Cambodia's unwieldy coalition government collapsed in violence on Saturday when Hun Sen's forces moved against Ranariddh's men in the capital. Ranariddh had left the country the previous day.
Hun Sen declared Ranariddh's ouster on Sunday as his forces were pushing Ranariddh's men from their bases in and around the city.
Ranariddh on Thursday urged the U.N. Security Council not to recognise any government emerging from the weekend's coup and also called for a freeze in aid to his country.

Ranariddh, speaking to reporters in New York after talks with Security Council President Peter Osvald of Sweden, said he had also asked the council to appeal for mediation in the crisis by his father, King Norodom Sihanouk, now in Beijing.

The international human rights group Amnesty International said in a statement on Thursday there was "compelling evidence of a targeted campaign (by Hun Sen's forces) to eliminate political opponents."

Government officials earlier this week confirmed that one senior Ranariddh loyalist had been arrested by Hun Sen's troops and later shot dead. There were unconfirmed reports of several other Ranariddh men being killed.
Many members of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party have left the country while others remained in hiding in the capital.
The United States said on Wednesday it was pulling 40 diplomats and their dependents out of the country and also urged between 1,000 and 1,300 other Americans to leave.

Several thousand foreigners have left Cambodia since Phnom Penh's battered airport reopened on Tuesday and Australia began the evacuation of up to 600 of its citizens, plus Canadians, New Zealanders and Swedes on Friday.

By midday, the first of six Australian Air Force evacuation flights had left Phnom Penh, witnesses said. Japan, Cambodia's biggest aid donor, said on Friday it was sending three Air Force transport planes to Thailand in preparation of a possible evacuation of its citizens.
The United States announced on Thursday it was suspending its aid programme for Cambodia for at least 30 days in response to Hun Sen's ouster of Ranariddh.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the move was "a clear signal to Hun Sen and his associates that the U.S. will not be conducting business as usual with those individuals."
Germany also said it suspended its aid and Australia said it was reviewing its policy.
The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) said on Thursday it still recongnised Ranariddh as co-premier and it was delaying Cambodia's entry into the grouping indefinitely.

Cambodia was due to become a full member of ASEAN at the end of the month. ASEAN currently groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Burma and Laos will become members later this month.
Shortly before the announcement Hun Sen warned against any interference in Cambodia's internal affairs. A spokesman for Hun Sen later said ASEAN's decision was regrettable.
Ordinary Cambodians said on Thursday their hopes of peace and prosperity were being dashed.

"Cambodia will be alone in the region. We'll get poorer and poorer. Most people thought Cambodia was getting richer and would live in peace and stability, but now the exact opposite is happening," university student Chin Sophea told Reuters.
